They live in the repository next to the monitors, and the alert text is generated from the same file so that they cannot disagree. A monitor without a runbook fails the definition check.
acceptanceCriteria: Alerts include a runbook link
Runbook names the owner and first checks

items.title: Access control and governance
items.description:
Control over who can see personal data and a trustworthy record of who did. This covers masking of personal columns by default, retention limits that delete data when we have no reason to keep it, an audit log that cannot be edited by the people it describes, and role mapping from the identity provider.

Governance used to mean a spreadsheet kept by one person. This feature moves each of its rows into something the platform enforces: classification tags, masking, retention and the audit log. The test of success is that an auditor's question can be answered from the system within an hour.

None of it should slow analysts down who have a legitimate need; access requests go through the existing request form and are granted within a day.

items.title: Mask personal columns by default
items.description:
Columns tagged as personal data are masked for everyone except groups explicitly granted access. Masking shows a partial value for emails, hashes identifiers consistently so joins still work, and returns null for free-text fields. The tag lives on the column definition, so a new column cannot become visible by accident.

Masking is applied in the query layer, not in the stored data, so a person who is granted access sees real values immediately and without a copy being made. The masked view of a table is the default view; the raw one is a separate object that only granted groups can select from.

Every grant has an expiry date and an owner who confirms it each quarter.
acceptanceCriteria: Tagged columns are masked unless the group is granted access
Hashed identifiers still join across tables
Free-text personal fields return null when masked
A column without a tag in the personal schema fails validation

comments.body: Salt rotation is yearly; joins across a rotation boundary need the old salt kept readable by the masking service only.

items.title: Consistent salted hash function
items.description:
Implement the keyed hash used for identifiers, with the key in the secrets manager and a documented rotation procedure.

The hash is an HMAC-SHA256 over the normalised identifier, truncated to 24 characters for readability in joins. Normalisation lowercases emails and strips whitespace, because the same person typed differently should hash to the same token.

items.title: Retention limits and scheduled deletion
items.description:
Each dataset declares how long it may be kept. A nightly job deletes expired partitions and records what it deleted. Deletion requests from customers are handled by a separate flow that finds the identifier through the lineage and removes or anonymises rows in every downstream table.

Legal holds override the schedule: a dataset with an active hold is skipped and the skip is logged with the hold reference.
acceptanceCriteria: Expired partitions are deleted nightly and logged
Datasets under legal hold are skipped and logged
Customer deletion reaches every downstream table

items.title: Audit log of data access
items.description:
Record every query against tagged tables with the person, the time, the tables and the row count. The log is written to a separate store that the platform team can append to but cannot modify, and is searchable by person and by table for the quarterly access review.

The log tables are partitioned by month and kept for seven years in cheap storage. The access review reads from a monthly summary rather than from the raw rows. Service accounts are logged like people, with the owning team recorded against them.
acceptanceCriteria: Every query on tagged tables is logged
The log store is append-only for the platform team
Searchable by person and by table

comments.body: Idea to log full query text. Dropped: the text can contain personal data itself.

items.title: Role mapping gives former team members access for a week after they move
items.description:
Group membership is synced from the identity provider once a week, so someone who moves from sales to finance keeps their old region access and gains the new one. Access reviews flagged six such cases. Sync should run hourly and removal should take effect immediately when the identity provider sends a group change event.

The incident was found in the quarterly review, not by an alert. The weekly sync job was originally written when team moves were rare; with the reorganisation this year there were forty-odd. Two of the six cases involved personal data in the finance schema, which is why this is a bug rather than an improvement.

The event stream from the identity provider already exists and is used by the intranet; subscribe to it rather than polling more often.
acceptanceCriteria: Group removals take effect within an hour
Group change events apply immediately
items.reproSteps:
1. Move a test user from the EMEA group to the finance group in the identity provider.
2. Open a regional dashboard as that user.
3. Observe the old EMEA data still visible.

comments.body: Identity provider event stream is documented on the intranet team wiki; the topic name is the same in staging.

items.title: Quarterly access review report
items.description:
Generate for each dataset owner a list of who has access and when they last used it, so the review is a ten minute task instead of a spreadsheet exercise.

The report is one table per dataset owner: person, group through which access is granted, last query date and number of queries in the quarter. People who have not used a dataset for ninety days are suggested for removal, and the owner confirms or declines with a single reply.
acceptanceCriteria: One list per dataset owner
Shows last use per person

items.title: Storage and cost
items.description:
Keeping the warehouse affordable without making anyone's life harder: partitioning large tables, compacting small files, finding tables that nobody reads and showing each team what their data costs.

The warehouse bill has doubled in a year while the number of active users has not. Most of the growth is storage that nobody looks at: raw files that were never compacted, partitions that should have expired and copies of tables made for an investigation two years ago.

The feature gives each team a view of what its data costs and the tools to shrink it safely.

items.title: Table bloat on the curated orders table slows the nightly merge
items.description:
The merge step for the orders table has gone from 12 minutes to 55 over three months. Dead tuples have piled up because the merge updates most rows daily and autovacuum cannot keep pace on a table of this size. Index size has doubled, and the plan for the merge join now spills to disk. A manual vacuum helps for a few days.

We should partition the table by order month so that the merge only touches recent partitions, and tune autovacuum for the hot ones, and measure the merge time before and after.

Numbers from the run history: 12 minutes in July, 31 minutes in September, 55 minutes last week. Table size grew from 90 GB to 210 GB over the same period while the live row count rose by only ten percent. The nightly merge updates most rows that are less than a month old, and each update leaves a dead tuple behind.

One side observation from the plan output: the merge join now spills hash batches to temporary files in the database temp directory, which is why the volume alerts on the database host started firing at 03:00.
acceptanceCriteria: The nightly merge for orders finishes in under 20 minutes
Only recent partitions are rewritten
Autovacuum settings are documented per partition class
Merge duration is measured and recorded before and after each step
items.reproSteps:
1. Check the duration of the orders merge over the last 90 days in the run history.
2. Compare dead tuple counts for the orders table before and after a manual vacuum.
3. Note that the duration returns to the old trend within a week.
5. Run EXPLAIN on the merge statement and note the hash batches spilling to temporary files.

comments.body: Rewriting the table online with pg_repack worked in staging and cut the size by 40 percent; we still need partitioning for the long term.
Autovacuum thresholds for the hot partitions set to 1 percent scale factor in staging; the merge time dropped by a third.

items.title: Partition orders by order month
items.description: Create the partitioned table, migrate in monthly slices during the quiet window and swap the names.

items.title: Compact small files in the raw zone
items.description:
Streaming connectors write many small files, which makes reads slow and storage listing expensive. A nightly compaction merges files of a day into a few large ones and removes the originals only after the new file has been verified by its row count.

The compaction target is files of 256 MB to 1 GB, which is where the warehouse reads fastest. It runs after the nightly load and before the morning reports, writing into a new location and swapping the table pointer atomically. The old files stay for an hour for readers that have already planned against them.
acceptanceCriteria: Daily files are merged into files of 256 MB or more
Originals are removed only after the row count matches

comments.body: First compaction of the marketing events day went from 41,000 files to 18.
Compaction target size changed from 128 MB to 256 MB after the read benchmarks.

items.title: Warehouse cost per team dashboard
items.description:
Break the monthly warehouse bill down by team using query tags and storage ownership, and show the trend. The aim is not chargeback but awareness: teams that see their own line item tend to remove their own forgotten tables.

Query tags are set by the dashboards and scheduled reports so that cost can be attributed even though every query runs as the same service account. Interactive work is tagged with the person's team from the identity provider. Untagged cost is shown as its own line, which tends to encourage tagging.
acceptanceCriteria: Cost per team per month with a trend
Storage and compute shown separately

items.title: Find unused tables
items.description: List curated tables with no reads in 90 days together with their size and owner, and email the owners a monthly digest suggesting archival.
acceptanceCriteria: Tables unread for 90 days are listed with size and owner
Owners receive a monthly digest

items.title: Bring back the old data catalogue
items.description: Removed: replaced by the metric catalogue and lineage view, which cover what people actually used the old catalogue for.

items.title: Compaction job deletes a day partition while a reader holds it
items.description:
The cleanup step removes originals immediately after compaction, so a long-running query that had already planned against the old files fails with a missing file error. Delay physical deletion by one hour after the swap so running queries can finish.

It was found when the quarterly finance report failed twice in a row at the same step. The failures lined up exactly with the compaction window, and the missing file named in the error was always one that compaction had just replaced.

A grace period of an hour is a pragmatic answer; a proper snapshot isolation would be better but depends on a warehouse feature we do not have yet.
acceptanceCriteria: Originals are kept for an hour after the swap
No reader sees a missing file error
items.reproSteps:
1. Start a long query over yesterday's raw events.
2. Trigger the compaction for that day.
3. Wait for the query to read the next file.
4. The query fails with a missing file error.

items.title: Runbook for restoring a dropped partition
items.description:
Document how to restore a partition from the daily snapshot and test the procedure against staging once per quarter.

The procedure has to be tested because a runbook that has never been run does not work. Each quarter someone who did not write it follows it on staging, records how long it took and fixes whatever was unclear.
